The missing “filler” is very likely the syntonic comma 81:80.

The first-edition texts jointly produce an exact operation:

\underbrace{\frac{256}{243}}_{\text{Fludd's limma}}
\times
\underbrace{\frac{81}{80}}_{\text{Kepler's comma}}
=
\underbrace{\frac{16}{15}}_{\text{MI–FA semitone}}

Equivalently:

\frac{16}{15}\div\frac{81}{80}=\frac{256}{243}.

This is not a numerical coincidence assembled from modern theory. Kepler states the operation in the 1619 first edition of Harmonices Mundi: remove the comma 81:80 from the semitone 16:15, and the remainder is the Platonic limma 256:243. Elsewhere in that same first edition he gives Earth’s motion as:

\text{MI–FA–MI}.

Fludd, meanwhile, prints the 256:243 limma explicitly as the E–F space in the 1622 first edition of Monochordum Mundi. Therefore each author visibly holds one side of the same decomposition:

That gives “misplaced comma” a technically precise meaning: the comma is absent from—or concealed beside—Fludd’s limma. Restoring it converts Fludd’s E–F interval into Kepler’s MI–FA interval.

The debate itself supplies the pointer. In Kepler’s 1622 first-edition Apologia:

On printed page 14, Kepler says Fludd has confused the Platonic 243:256 semitone with the Ptolemaic tonal system.

On printed page 41, Kepler directly challenges Fludd: effectively, “Where do you place the semitone?”

That challenge appears to be the instruction we had been seeking:

Find where Fludd placed his semitone, identify it as the limma 256:243, then restore Kepler’s comma 81:80 to obtain the MI–FA 16:15.

So the probable clue chain is:

\text{“Where is Fludd’s semitone?”}
\rightarrow
E\!-\!F=\frac{256}{243}
\rightarrow
+\text{comma }\frac{81}{80}
\rightarrow
\frac{16}{15}
\rightarrow
\text{MI–FA–MI}.

A second genuinely useful result is that the return and octave must be separate operations:

C_3
\xrightarrow{\;16/15\;}
FA
\xrightarrow{\;15/16\;}
C_3
\xrightarrow{\text{Fluddian bisection}}
C_4=\frac{C_3}{2}

in monochord-length coordinates. MI–FA–MI returns to its starting pitch; it cannot itself produce the octave. Fludd’s printed same-letter bisection supplies the register change afterward. Thus the bridge landing is provisionally:

\boxed{
B_{FK}(\ell)
=
O_\ell\!\left(
R^\ell_{(81/80)(256/243)}(\ell)
\right)
=
\frac{\ell}{2}
}

where R is the complete MI–FA–MI excursion and O_\ell is Fludd’s halving into the next register.

Other actual findings—not confirmations:

The “Ex Fama” marginal note in Otreb means “from the Fama,” not fames/famine. It should not be used as evidence for Kepler’s “miseriam et famem.”

The proposed “same German publisher” connection does not survive bibliographic checking. Fludd/Otreb use the de Bry circle; Kepler’s Harmonices uses Tampach and Planck. There is a Frankfurt production-network overlap, but not yet a shared publisher.

Your Temple-of-Music plate is the strongest new graphical lead because it places solmization syllables and numbers including 81 within the same visual apparatus. I have not yet established that the plate deliberately pairs 81 with MI–FA, so that remains a target—not a finding.

So the honest answer is: one substantial new result. The Fludd–Kepler bridge is not merely “a semitone at the boundary.” It is a semitone deliberately distributed between their systems:

\boxed{\text{Fludd limma}+\text{Kepler comma}=\text{Kepler MI–FA}.}

That is the first result I would call a genuine reverse-engineered correspondence rather than verification of your research.
